topic: What makes a website read as AI-generated / templated vs. designed by a person with taste — with 2025-26 designer commentary and first-hand CSS forensics on editorial exemplars — producing a banned-signals list, a real-designer-signals list, and a shippable taste rubric for satishregonda.in.
key_findings: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT FINDING: the AI tell has MOVED. Purple-to-blue gradients are the 2023-25 tell. Kyle Chayka's New Yorker column (June 2026, summarized on his Substack, which I fetched) identifies the CURRENT default house style as: beige/cream backgrounds, rusty-orange accents, large italicized serif headlines, subheads with wide letterspacing ("tracked out"), ticker-like scrolling text bars "as if the website were a cable-news show," and rounded rectangle outlines with neon glow underneath. This is the trap for THIS project: the naive brief "minimal, editorial, cream paper, serif type" lands exactly on the 2026 AI default unless every one of those moves is executed differently.

Designer Celine Nguyen, quoted in that reporting: "Now I find myself instinctively repulsed by the warm tones even though I love this kind of color palette." The palette is not bad; its unearned deployment is. Matt Ström-Awn: the model's "preferences and tendencies and aesthetics are deeply baked into its machinery; it is always going to struggle to produce something that doesn't look like A.I."

FORENSIC EVIDENCE (I curled the CSS myself): asteriskmag.com's entire stylesheet (assets/css/style.css, 43,332 bytes) contains ZERO occurrences of `box-shadow` and ZERO border-radius rules other than `--ckb-btn-radius: 0`. worksinprogress.co's Layout.BaZiK8iM.css is 213,935 bytes and contains `box-shadow` exactly TWICE, with `border-radius:0` appearing more often than any nonzero value. press.stripe.com and pudding.cool: zero box-shadow. Card shadows are not how good editorial sites make depth — hairline rules are.

Asterisk's grid columns are deliberately asymmetric: `2fr 4fr 2fr 3fr 1.5fr`, `1fr 2fr 1fr .5fr`, `2fr 1fr 1fr`, alongside a main article grid of `var(--asterisk-width) minmax(min-content, 30rem) minmax(...)`. Works in Progress uses `grid-template-columns: var(--desktop-primary-area-fr, 94fr) 63fr 0fr` — a 94:63 split — plus `subgrid`. AI output overwhelmingly emits `repeat(3, 1fr)`. Uneven fr ratios are a machine-checkable signature of a human deciding proportions.

Asterisk applies OPTICAL tracking, not global tracking: negative letter-spacing on display sizes (-0.05em, -0.03em, -0.02em, -0.01em) and positive on small/uppercase (+0.01em, +0.02em). This size-dependent inversion is the classic typographer's move and is almost never present in generated CSS, which either omits tracking or applies one value everywhere.

Real editorial sites set measure in characters, not pixels: Asterisk uses `max-width: 60ch` and `30ch`, plus `--maxwidth-text: 750px` / `60vw` / `50vw` with `--margin-left: calc((100vw - var(--maxwidth-text))*0.5)`. Butterick's Practical Typography (summary-of-key-rules) prescribes 15-25px body on the web, line spacing 120-145% of point size, and 45-90 characters per line.

Palettes are near-monochrome plus a tiny, deliberate accent set. Works in Progress: #121212 near-black (121 uses) on #fff7f4 warm paper (73 uses), with per-topic accents #f4d06f, #e20a39, #363b8f, #073429. Asterisk: --cream #faf8f0, --black #000000, --grey-dark #404040, --grey #99999a, --grey-light #d7d6cd (rules), and exactly one accent --blue #2d90cf. The Pudding: a ten-step gray ramp from rgb(247,247,247) to rgb(25,25,25) plus exactly two chromatic accents (#4717f6, #3AE660). Stripe Press's text color is #201819 — a WARM near-black, not #000.

Nobody good uses one typeface. Verified font stacks: Works in Progress = Editor (wedge serif, Indian Type Foundry, designed by Jean-Baptiste Morizot) + GT America Mono; Asterisk = Atlas Grotesk + Noe Text + Noe Standard; Stripe Press = Ivar Display / Ivar Headline / Ivar Text (one superfamily across three OPTICAL SIZES); Aeon = Atlas Grotesk + Atlas Typewriter + Academica + Stratos + PP Right Grotesk; The Pudding = Atlas Grotesk + Atlas Typewriter + Tiempos Text + Gooper SemiCondensed; Nautilus = Freight Sans + Freight Display; Anthropic's transformer-circuits.pub = Styrene A + Tiempos Text; Epoch AI = Messina Sans; New Yorker = Adobe Caslon Pro + Irvin (bespoke) + Neutraface + Graphik.

gwern.net is the strongest example of "idiosyncratic but consistent": Source Serif 4 + Source Sans 3 + IBM Plex Mono for the system, PLUS six historical drop-cap faces (Cheshire Initials, Deutsche Zierschrift, Goudy Initialen, Great Primer Uncials, Kanzlei Initialen, Yinit) rotated per essay, plus `font-feature-settings: 'ss01'` / `'ss02','ss03'`, `font-variant-caps: small-caps`, `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` and `lining-nums`. OpenType feature usage is a near-perfect proxy for a human having been present.

The Tailwind indigo lineage is documented: Tailwind UI shipped `bg-indigo-500` as the neutral placeholder in component examples; thousands of tutorials and templates copied it; LLMs trained on that corpus learned "modern web = purple." Adam Wathan has publicly apologized for it (reported across dev.to and prg.sh writeups). The fix named repeatedly is not to *extend* the Tailwind color key but to DELETE it so there is no `indigo-600` to fall back to.

The developersdigest "16 AI design slop patterns" list, fetched in full, names: Inter everywhere; the Space Grotesk / Instrument Serif / Geist combo; a serif italic used as the accent for one hero word in an otherwise-Inter page; "VibeCode Purple"; permanent dark mode with medium-grey body text; barely-passing contrast; gradients everywhere; large colored glows and colored box-shadows; centered hero; a badge directly above the H1; colored left-border stripes on cards; identical feature cards with an icon on top; numbered 1-2-3 step sequences; stat banners; emoji nav sidebars; all-caps section labels.

Nielsen Norman Group research on scroll-triggered text animations records a participant saying: "I don't like how everything comes together when I'm scrolling down… I hate that it has to load every single section. Sometimes I just want to see information there without having to see a cool little movement." NN/g's rules: never animate primary body text, only secondary graphics; fire once, never on return navigation; task-focused audiences (medical, financial, B2B — and by extension academic) resist decorative motion most.

The AI copy voice is now a named, listed phenomenon. Ström-Awn's "expansion artifacts" essay names hedging verbs and fuzzing adjectives (delve, intricate, tapestry, multifaceted) and the setup/payoff/signposted-takeaway structure ("This matters because…"). Post-ChatGPT frequency-spiking words include commendable, meticulous, pivotal, showcasing, robust, seamless, leverage, harness, streamline, empower, elevate, unlock. The "It's not just X — it's Y" construction and "in the ever-evolving landscape" are the loudest tells.

Glassmorphism's core failure is that contrast becomes DYNAMIC: text over a blurred translucent panel can pass WCAG on one part of the backdrop and fail on another, so it cannot be statically verified. That's a disqualifying property for an institutional site, independent of taste.

AI image tells have shifted too: six fingers and waxy skin are largely fixed by 2026. What still fails is background text (storefronts, book spines, license plates, packaging small print), repeated/cloned faces in crowds, inconsistent shadow directions, and missing C2PA/SynthID provenance. For an academic site this is moot in the best way — any AI image at all is a credibility hit.

Tufte CSS (tufte.css, 9,494 bytes) sets body text to `max-width: 55%` and sidenotes to `40%`, with `et-book` as the text face — i.e., a deliberately ASYMMETRIC page where the right margin is functional, not empty. gwern's sidenote essay quotes Bringhurst: "Sidenotes give more life and variety to the page and are the easiest of all to find and read," and documents that sidenotes collide below ~1024px so a mobile fallback (inline expansion or collapse) is mandatory.

There is a real, project-relevant typographic opportunity: Works in Progress's reading face, Editor, is from the Indian Type Foundry (Ahmedabad, founded 2009, 200+ families across 20 writing systems, Kohinoor in the Design Museum's permanent collection). ITF's free service Fontshare (Erode, Sentient, Switzer, Zodiak, Satoshi, Gambetta, Bespoke Serif) ships under the ITF Free Font License, which per multiple secondary sources permits commercial and webfont use with self-hosting or CDN. An Indian professor's site set in an Indian foundry's type is a real editorial reason, not an arbitrary one — and it is not what a model would default to.

The bar in academic web design is extremely low, which is an advantage. I checked the 2025 Best Personal Academic Websites Contest winners: madeline-eppley.com renders in `Arial, sans-serif`; phresonance.com is WordPress on Manrope; fawadnajam.com is WordPress 6.7.7; cecibaldoni.github.io is Quarto in Roboto Mono; kamsekar.github.io is Jekyll. None make a typographic argument. A genuinely typeset site will be visibly unlike every peer site in the field.

Fonts In Use data has been quantified: a Scientific Reports paper (Nature, s41598-024-81601-w) analyzed 22,897 font-use cases and 9,022 fonts scraped from fontsinuse.com across 19 design mediums to build an empirical typeface-pairing network — evidence that pairing conventions are measurable, not vibes.

Modern CSS now ships a typesetter's toolkit that is off by default, and switching it on is itself a taste signal: `text-wrap: balance` on headings (Chrome 114+, Firefox 121+, Safari 17.5+), `text-wrap: pretty` on body (Chrome 117+, Safari 17.5+), `font-optical-sizing: auto`, `initial-letter` (Chrome 110+, Safari via -webkit-, no Firefox), `hanging-punctuation: first` (Safari 10+ only — needs a `text-indent: -0.42em` fallback), `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for tables of years and discharge values.
recommendations: Write the palette down BEFORE any component, and make it near-monochrome plus exactly one accent. Concretely: a warm near-black around #1A1918-#201819 (never #000000 for body text at large areas, never pure #FFFFFF ground), a paper tone, one rule-grey, one muted grey for metadata, and ONE chromatic accent. Delete Tailwind's `colors` key entirely rather than extending it, so there is no `indigo-600` to fall back to. Model this on Asterisk's six-token system (--cream #faf8f0, --black, --grey-dark #404040, --grey #99999a, --grey-light #d7d6cd, --blue #2d90cf).

AVOID the cream + rust-orange + italic-serif combination specifically. It is now the single most recognizable AI signature of 2026. If you want a warm ground, go somewhere the model doesn't: a cool paper (a hair of blue-grey, e.g. around #F4F5F3), or a true off-white with a warm near-black text that does the warming. Give the accent a SOURCED reason and say so in the design notes — e.g. sampled from an IMD rainfall-classification ramp, or from a Musi/Godavari gauge chart, or from Deccan trap basalt. A reason you can name is what a template cannot have.

Pair two families with an argument, and use a third only for metadata. Strong project-specific option: Erode or Sentient (Indian Type Foundry, free via Fontshare) for reading, Switzer for UI/navigation, and a mono for dates, issue numbers, DOIs and figure captions — mirroring Works in Progress's Editor + GT America Mono. The reason to write down: ITF is an Indian foundry and this is an Indian institution's site. Free/no-risk alternative with equal credibility: Source Serif 4 + Source Sans 3 + IBM Plex Mono (gwern's exact stack). If budget allows, license one real text face (Tiempos Text, Freight Text, Ivar Text) — the whole site's character comes from it.

BAN Inter as the only face, and ban the specific 2026 AI stacks: Space Grotesk + Instrument Serif, Playfair Display headings over a clean sans, and the single-italic-serif-accent-word hero. Playfair in 2026 reads as "I used the first nice-looking Google serif I found."

Build depth from HAIRLINE RULES, not shadows. Target: `box-shadow` appears 0-2 times in the whole stylesheet (Asterisk: 0; Works in Progress: 2 in 214KB). Use `1px solid` in a token that is a real color — Asterisk uses `1px solid var(--c-text)`, i.e. full-strength black rules, not `rgba(0,0,0,0.08)`. Set border-radius to 0 as the default and allow exceptions only where a photograph or a form control genuinely needs it.

Make ONE deliberate asymmetry and repeat it everywhere. Pick an uneven ratio for the page — e.g. `grid-template-columns: 94fr 63fr` (Works in Progress) or a Tufte-style `55% text / 40% margin` — and use the narrow column functionally: publication years, co-author lists, dataset links, figure captions, sidenotes on the blog. Never emit `repeat(3, 1fr)` for a content section. The margin column is what will make this site unlike every other academic site.

Let real data be the only ornament. A hydrologist has an asset no template and no model can fake: actual hydrographs, rainfall time series, flood-extent footprints, gauge records. One hairline line-chart of real Musi or Godavari discharge, drawn as SVG in the accent color at 1px, is worth more than any hero image, any illustration, and any abstract blob. It also makes the site self-evidently his.

Keep the professor's actual sentences. His current site says "after masters at the IIT Kanpur, I pursued PhD at the University of Colorado at Boulder" and describes wanting "a holistic approach for better scientific understanding of surface hydrology and developing efficient solutions/tools that makes human life better." Keep the first person, keep the specific institutions, keep the slightly non-idiomatic article usage. The instant you rewrite it into "Dr. Regonda is a leading researcher advancing our understanding of…" the page becomes generic. Copy-edit for clarity, never for polish.

Every content type must render SPECIFICS, not adjectives. Design the Google Sheets schema so specifics can't be lost: publications get separate columns for year, journal, volume, DOI, co-authors; students get start year, degree, thesis title, current position, and (for alumni) year left; news gets a real date. A page that says "March 2024 · Journal of Hydrology · with A. Kumar and S. Rao · doi:10.1016/…" cannot be mistaken for a template. A page that says "Cutting-edge research in water resources" always will.

Motion budget: essentially zero. No scroll-triggered fade-ins on body content, no AOS, no stagger, no counters. NN/g's finding is that task-focused audiences resent it most, and an academic audience is maximally task-focused. Permitted: link underline transitions, a focus ring, and at most one first-load reveal on the masthead. Honor `prefers-reduced-motion` regardless.

Turn on the CSS typesetting features as progressive enhancement: `text-wrap: balance` on h1-h3, `text-wrap: pretty` on p, `font-optical-sizing: auto` if the face has an opsz axis, `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on the publications and students tables so years align in a column, `lining-nums` in headings, small-caps for the section eyebrows instead of tracked-out all-caps, and `hanging-punctuation: first` with a `text-indent: -0.42em` fallback for pull quotes.

Use real photography of real places and real people: the RAFT team in the field, gauges, drones, the Musi in flood, the lab, whiteboards. Underexposed, slightly imperfect, correctly captioned with place and date. Zero stock. Zero AI-generated imagery of any kind — an academic site trades on evidentiary credibility and a generated image is a direct hit to it. If a photo is missing, use type and a rule; never a placeholder illustration.

Set body type at 18-20px with line-height ~1.55 and measure at 62-68ch on the article/blog template, per Butterick's 15-25px / 120-145% / 45-90 characters. Set nav, metadata and captions in the mono or small-caps at 13-14px with +0.02em tracking. Set display sizes with NEGATIVE tracking (-0.02em to -0.04em). If the tracking is the same at 14px and 56px, a human did not set it.

Give the site one idiosyncratic, consistent detail that is cheap to maintain and impossible to template — gwern's rotating historical drop caps are the model. Candidates here: a per-page hairline hydrograph in the margin whose shape comes from a real record; issue-style numbering on blog posts ("No. 014"); the asterisk-slot device Asterisk uses (`--asterisk-width: 50px`) repurposed as a small water-level glyph in the left rail; or dates always set as "14 Aug 2024" in mono. Pick one. Repeat it on every page.

Ship a machine-checkable design contract in the repo (a DESIGN.md plus a grep script), because content will be edited over years and the defaults will creep back. Assert: zero `box-shadow` outside an allowlist; zero `linear-gradient` on text or backgrounds; zero `rounded-2xl`; zero `#6366F1`/`#4F46E5`/indigo/violet tokens; font-family only from the two declared families plus mono; no `repeat(3, 1fr)` in section layout; no emoji in headings or nav.

Do a final read-aloud pass on all copy against a banned-words list: elevate, unlock, empower, leverage, harness, streamline, seamless, robust, cutting-edge, transformative, holistic (in the marketing sense), "ever-evolving," "at the intersection of," "passionate about," "Let's connect!", "It's not just X — it's Y." Also cut all exclamation points except at most one in the whole site, per Butterick.
pitfalls: Landing on the 2026 AI default while trying to avoid the 2023 one. "Cream background + rust/terracotta accent + big italic serif headline + tracked-out uppercase eyebrow + a scrolling news ticker" IS the current Claude/LLM house style per Chayka's reporting. Executing the brief's word 'editorial' literally will produce exactly this. Every one of those five moves needs a deliberate deviation.

Thinking 'minimal' means 'empty.' Generated minimalism = a centered headline, huge vertical padding, and nothing to look at. Real editorial minimalism is DENSE: Works in Progress and Asterisk pack bylines, issue numbers, topic tags, rules and running heads into tight, information-rich blocks. Emptiness reads as having nothing to say; density with hierarchy reads as authority.

Three-column icon-and-title grids for research areas. This is the single most template-coded layout on the web and it is where an academic site will reach first ("Hydroclimatology / Flood Forecasting / Urban Flooding" in three rounded cards with Lucide droplet, cloud and building icons). Kill it. Use a numbered editorial list with real one-sentence descriptions and a real figure, or an asymmetric two-column with the margin carrying years and papers.

Emoji as section markers or in nav. Judges in the 2025 academic-website contest explicitly flagged emoji as an accessibility problem on an otherwise-winning site, and 'emoji nav sidebars' is item 15 on the AI-slop list. On a professor's site they also read as slightly juvenile in an Indian institutional context.

Stat counters that count up: "50+ Publications · 12 Students · 8 Projects." Meaningless numbers presented as achievements is a SaaS move. Real numbers belong inline and in context: "Regional flood forecasts issued for the Musi basin since 2019" beats a counter. If you must show counts, show them as static text in tabular figures, never animated.

Glassmorphism or any translucent panel over imagery. Its contrast is dynamic and therefore cannot be verified against WCAG AA — text can pass over one part of a backdrop and fail over another. Disqualifying for an institutional page regardless of aesthetics.

Over-even spacing. If every gap on the page is 8/16/24/32/48/64 with nothing in between and no optical corrections, the page reads as generated even when nothing else is wrong. Optical spacing means a heading sits closer to the paragraph it owns than to the one above it; that a rule sits 6px below a cap-height line rather than 8; that a photo caption hangs 2px tight. Budget time for nudging.

A hero with a centered headline and two CTA buttons ('View Publications' / 'Contact Me'). Academic sites have no CTAs. The top of the page should be his name, his position, one sentence in his own words, and the first real thing — a recent paper, a photo from the field, a current opening.

Letting the Google Sheets CMS flatten specificity. If the sheet has one 'description' column per item, editors will type adjectives into it. Force specifics with typed columns (year, venue, DOI, co-authors, place, date) so the template renders facts even when the person filling it in writes vaguely.

Over-designing the blog into a magazine. He is a busy professor; posts will be short and irregular. A layout that needs a hero image and a 200-word standfirst per post will look broken after the third post. Design the blog for a 300-word text-only post first, and let images be optional enhancements.

Using a serif with no italic or no real small caps. Many free display serifs (Playfair aside) ship without proper italics or with fake small caps. Butterick: 'If you don't have real small caps, don't use them at all.' Check the font's italic, small-cap and tabular-figure support before committing — the publications list will need tabular figures and the citations will need italics.

Dark mode by default with medium-grey body text. 'Permanent dark mode with medium-grey body text and all-caps section labels' is a named slop pattern. If dark mode is offered, it must be a deliberate second palette with the same contrast discipline, not an inverted afterthought.

Sidenotes without a mobile plan. Sidenotes are the best print-borrowed device available and they collide with body text below ~1024px. Decide the fallback (inline expansion vs. collapse-on-tap) before building, or don't use them.

AI-generated 'scientific' imagery — abstract water renders, generated satellite-looking maps, illustrated droplet motifs. In a field where the currency is verifiable observation, a fabricated image is a substantive credibility problem, not just a stylistic one.

Cargo-culting brutalism as the escape hatch. Overcorrecting into raw Times New Roman, harsh borders and Comic-Sans-adjacent irony reads as a different kind of costume and undercuts the seriousness the client needs. The target is 'quietly, expensively typeset,' not 'defiantly ugly.'

exemplars.name: Works in Progress (magazine; site design by And—Now, London)
exemplars.what_works: A rigorous two-face system — Editor (wedge serif, Indian Type Foundry, by Jean-Baptiste Morizot) for reading, GT America Mono Light/Bold for all secondary information — over a warm paper ground. Verified in Layout.BaZiK8iM.css: text #121212 on #fff7f4, per-topic accent colors (#f4d06f, #e20a39, #363b8f, #073429, plus tinted grounds #f8e6ea, #d8d9f1, #cee0dc) that code the subject rather than decorate it, `box-shadow` used exactly twice in 214KB, border-radius overwhelmingly 0, `grid-template-columns: 94fr 63fr 0fr` and `subgrid`, `font-variant: small-caps`, and letter-spacing (.08em/.05em) applied only to uppercase. Issues are numbered; each issue gets commissioned illustration from a different artist. The studio's stated brand values are Accessible, Academic, Inspiring — the exact register this project needs.
exemplars.steal_this: The mono-for-metadata rule. Set every date, issue number, topic tag, DOI, figure label and byline in a mono at 13px; set everything readable in the serif. It is one decision, it is free, it is instantly legible as a design system, and it is the opposite of what a model emits.

exemplars.name: Asterisk Magazine
exemplars.what_works: The purest evidence I found. assets/css/style.css is 43,332 bytes and contains ZERO box-shadow and no border-radius except `--ckb-btn-radius: 0`. Six color tokens total: --cream #faf8f0, --black #000000, --grey-dark #404040, --grey #99999a, --grey-light #d7d6cd, one accent --blue #2d90cf (+ --blue-light #abd3ec). Measure declared in characters (`max-width: 60ch`, `30ch`) and as `--maxwidth-text: 750px / 60vw / 50vw` with `--margin-left: calc((100vw - var(--maxwidth-text))*0.5)`. Grids are deliberately uneven: `2fr 4fr 2fr 3fr 1.5fr`, `1fr 2fr 1fr .5fr`. Borders are `1px solid var(--c-text)` — full-strength rules, not 8%-alpha greys. Tracking inverts by size: -0.05em/-0.03em/-0.02em on display, +0.01em/+0.02em on small. Type: Atlas Grotesk + Noe Text + Noe Standard.
exemplars.steal_this: Two rules, adopted literally: (1) hairlines are `1px solid` in the TEXT color, not a translucent grey — it is the single cheapest thing that separates print-trained from template design; (2) invert letter-spacing by size, negative on display and positive on small caps/labels.

exemplars.name: Stripe Press
exemplars.what_works: One superfamily used across three optical sizes — Ivar Display, Ivar Headline, Ivar Text (Letters from Sweden) — which is a strictly typographic way to build hierarchy without adding families or weights. Zero box-shadow. Body color #201819: a warm, slightly red near-black rather than #000, which makes the page feel like ink on paper. Letter-spacing tuned to .32px on specific elements.
exemplars.steal_this: Never use pure #000 on pure #FFF. Pick a warm near-black in the #1A1918-#201819 range and let it carry the paper feeling, so you don't have to reach for a cream background (which is now the AI tell).

exemplars.name: gwern.net (Gwern Branwen)
exemplars.what_works: The most craft-dense long-form academic site on the web. style.css is 310KB and declares Source Serif 4 + Source Sans 3 + IBM Plex Mono for the system, then adds six historical initial/drop-cap faces (Cheshire Initials, Deutsche Zierschrift, Goudy Initialen, Great Primer Uncials, Kanzlei Initialen, Yinit) rotated per essay. It switches on `font-feature-settings: 'ss01'` and `'ss02','ss03'`, `font-variant-caps: small-caps`, `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` and `lining-nums`, and sets `hyphens: none` deliberately. His companion essay on sidenotes catalogues every implementation and its mobile fallback.
exemplars.steal_this: One idiosyncratic ornament, applied systematically, plus real OpenType feature usage. Both are invisible to a casual reader and unmistakable to anyone who looks — which is exactly the definition of taste.

exemplars.name: Tufte CSS (Edward Tufte / Dave Liepmann)
exemplars.what_works: Establishes the asymmetric scholarly page as a web convention: body text at `max-width: 55%`, sidenotes at `40%`, set in et-book (a Bembo-descendant), with line-heights of 1.42 for body. The right margin is functional rather than empty — it carries notes, citations and small figures.
exemplars.steal_this: The functional margin. On a hydrology site, put the year, the co-authors, the dataset link, the basin name and the figure caption in a persistent narrow rail. It creates asymmetry that is earned by content, which is the only kind that survives.

exemplars.name: The Pudding
exemplars.what_works: Zero box-shadow. A ten-step named grey ramp (--color-gray-50 rgb(247,247,247) through --color-gray-1000 rgb(25,25,25)) with semantic aliases (--color-fg, --color-bg, --color-border, --color-link, --color-focus) and only TWO chromatic accents in the whole system: --color-blue #4717f6 and --color-electric-green #3AE660 (which doubles as the focus color). Four families with distinct jobs: Atlas Grotesk (sans), Atlas Typewriter (mono), Tiempos Text (serif body), Gooper SemiCondensed (display).
exemplars.steal_this: Semantic color naming over literal. Ship --color-fg / --color-bg / --color-border / --color-accent / --color-focus mapped onto a grey ramp, so the site can never accumulate ad-hoc greys and so a future palette change is one edit.

exemplars.name: Anthropic Transformer Circuits (research publication)
exemplars.what_works: Proof that a serious technical/scientific publication reads better with real type: Styrene A (Commercial Type) for sans and Tiempos Text (Klim) for reading, on a plain ground, with no cards, no shadows and no hero. Dense, figure-heavy scientific content laid out as an article rather than a landing page.
exemplars.steal_this: The information architecture: a research site is a LIST OF PAPERS, presented as an editorial index with dates and authors, not a marketing page with a 'Research' section containing three icon cards.

exemplars.name: Aeon
exemplars.what_works: A five-family editorial system with clearly divided labor — Academica (serif, book weights + italics) for reading, Atlas Grotesk for interface, Atlas Typewriter for metadata, Stratos and PP Right Grotesk Wide Medium for display. Fonts are subset and self-hosted (the -s.p. suffix in the woff2 filenames), which is a performance decision a person made.
exemplars.steal_this: Self-host and subset the webfonts (woff2, latin subset, `font-display: swap`, preload the two faces above the fold). It is faster than Google Fonts, it removes a third-party dependency, and it is the standard move of anyone who has actually shipped typography.

exemplars.name: Nautilus
exemplars.what_works: A science magazine running a single superfamily pair — Freight Sans (Book, SemiBold) and Freight Display (Book) — across the whole publication, with typography tokens named by ROLE (--font-family--body, --font-family--eyebrow, --font-family--nav, --font-family--post-meta) rather than by face. Directly relevant register: rigorous science written for an intelligent general audience.
exemplars.steal_this: Name type tokens by role (body / eyebrow / nav / meta / display), not by family. It forces you to decide what each piece of text IS before you decide what it looks like, and it survives a typeface change.

exemplars.name: The New Yorker
exemplars.what_works: Verified font payload includes TNYAdobeCaslonPro (Regular/Italic/Bold), IrvinText and Irvin Heading (the bespoke proprietary masthead face), NeutrafaceNewYorker-SemiBold, Graphik, Lora and Lato. The identity lives in one commissioned face that literally no one else can have.
exemplars.steal_this: Not the fonts — the principle. Find the one element of this site that cannot be copied and make it the identity. For a hydrologist that is his own data: a real hydrograph, drawn once, at 1px, reused as the site's signature mark.

exemplars.name: Kyle Chayka, 'The generic style of AI web design' (New Yorker column / Substack)
exemplars.what_works: The canonical 2026 statement of the problem, with named designers on record. Catalogues the current default: beige/cream grounds, rusty-orange accents, big italicized serifs, tracked-out subheads, cable-news-style tickers, rounded rectangle outlines with neon glow. Quotes Celine Nguyen ('instinctively repulsed by the warm tones even though I love this kind of color palette') and Matt Ström-Awn on the aesthetics being 'deeply baked into its machinery.'
exemplars.steal_this: Use it as the negative brief. Print the six traits and check the finished design against them — because this is the list the client's peers will unconsciously be pattern-matching against in 2026.

exemplars.name: Carmen Ansio, 'Editorial Typography in CSS'
exemplars.what_works: Concrete, current, copy-pasteable editorial CSS with a browser-support table: `text-wrap: balance` with `max-inline-size: 24ch` on headings; `text-wrap: pretty` with `32ch` on body; `initial-letter: 3` for drop caps (with -webkit- prefix, no Firefox); `font-optical-sizing: auto`; `hanging-punctuation: first` (Safari only) with a `text-indent: -0.42em` fallback; fluid scales via clamp().
exemplars.steal_this: The whole progressive-enhancement stance: ornamental typographic properties are added last, degrade to nothing, and cost zero when unsupported — so there is no excuse not to switch them on.

details:
## The one thing to internalise before anything else

**The AI tell moved, and it moved toward exactly the aesthetic this brief describes.**

Purple-to-blue gradients, glassmorphism and `rounded-2xl shadow-lg` are the *2023–2025* signature, traceable to Tailwind UI shipping `bg-indigo-500` as a neutral placeholder, which then saturated GitHub, Stack Overflow and every tutorial, which then became what models predict. That's still worth banning — but it is no longer the sharpest tell.

Kyle Chayka's New Yorker column (June 2026; I fetched his Substack version) documents the **current** default house style, and it is:

- beige and cream backgrounds
- rusty-orange / terracotta accents
- large serif typefaces, **italicised and highlighted**
- subheadings **tracked out** (wide letterspacing)
- **ticker-like scrolling text bars**, "as if the website were a cable-news show"
- dashboard blocks made of "multiple rounded rectangular outlines, sometimes with a neon glow underneath"
- "tasteful, slightly askew primary colors" — desaturated, mid-century-adjacent

On the record in that reporting:

> **Celine Nguyen:** "Now I find myself instinctively repulsed by the warm tones even though I love this kind of color palette."

> **Matt Ström-Awn:** "The preferences and tendencies and aesthetics are deeply baked into its machinery; it is always going to struggle to produce something that doesn't look like A.I."

> **Anthropic's own documentation**, as quoted: giving "generic instructions" such as *"don't use cream"* is likely to "shift the model to a different fixed palette rather than producing variety."

That last line is the operational warning. **Negative prompting doesn't produce taste; it produces a different default.** The only exit is positive, sourced, specific decisions — a named typeface with a reason, a colour with a provenance, a ratio you chose.

For this project: "modern, minimal, editorial, academic, cream paper, serif type" is *the AI attractor basin in 2026*. Every instinct that phrase produces has to be deliberately deflected.

---

## Forensic evidence: what good editorial sites actually do

I curled the stylesheets. These are counts from the real files, not impressions.

| Site | Stylesheet | Bytes | `box-shadow` | `border-radius` |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| Asterisk | `assets/css/style.css` | 43,332 | **0** | **0** (only `--ckb-btn-radius: 0`) |
| Works in Progress | `_astro/Layout.BaZiK8iM.css` | 213,935 | **2** | mostly `0`; 2× `10px`, 1× `2px`, 2× `50%` |
| Stripe Press | `v1-Page-…css` | 3,896 | **0** | 1 |
| The Pudding | `_app/immutable/assets/0.…css` | 26,423 | **0** | 6 |

**Depth in editorial design comes from hairline rules and value contrast, not shadows.** This is the most machine-checkable difference between a designed page and a generated one.

### Palettes (verbatim tokens)

**Asterisk** — six tokens, one accent:
```
--cream:      #faf8f0
--black:      #000000
--grey-dark:  #404040
--grey:       #99999a
--grey-light: #d7d6cd
--blue:       #2d90cf   --blue-light: #abd3ec
--c-bg: var(--cream);  --c-text: var(--black);  --c-text-muted: var(--grey)
```

**Works in Progress** — occurrence counts in the stylesheet:
```
#121212 ×121  (near-black text)
#fff7f4 ×73   (warm paper ground)
#f4d06f ×64   #e20a39 ×37   #363b8f ×37   #073429 ×36   (topic accents)
#f8e6ea ×35   #d8d9f1 ×34   #cee0dc ×34   (tinted grounds per topic)
```
The accents *encode the topic*; they aren't decoration.

**The Pudding** — a full grey ramp plus exactly two chromatic colours:
```
--color-gray-50: rgb(247,247,247) … --color-gray-1000: rgb(25,25,25)
--color-blue: #4717f6      --color-electric-green: #3AE660  (also --color-focus)
--color-fg / --color-bg / --color-border / --color-link / --color-button-bg  → aliased onto the ramp
```

**Stripe Press** body colour: `#201819` — a *warm* near-black. Not `#000`.

### Grids — deliberate asymmetry

**Asterisk:**
```css
grid-template-columns: 2fr 4fr 2fr 3fr 1.5fr;
grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr .5fr;
grid-template-columns: 2fr 1fr 1fr;
grid-template-columns: var(--asterisk-width) minmax(min-content, 30rem) minmax(min-content, …);
--asterisk-width: 50px;
```

**Works in Progress:**
```css
grid-template-columns: var(--desktop-primary-area-fr, 94fr) 63fr 0fr;
grid-template-columns: subgrid;
```

A 94:63 split. Someone chose that. `repeat(3, 1fr)` is what a model chooses.

### Measure

**Asterisk** declares measure in characters and viewport-relative widths, and derives its left margin from it:
```css
--maxwidth-text: 750px;   /* desktop */
--maxwidth-text: 60vw;  --maxwidth-text: 50vw;   /* breakpoints */
--margin-left: calc((100vw - var(--maxwidth-text)) * 0.5);
--indent: 2.5rem;
max-width: 60ch;   max-width: 30ch;
line-height: 1.4 (body) / 1.2 (display) / 1.6 (one context)
```

**Tufte CSS** (`tufte.css`, 9,494 bytes): body `max-width: 55%`, sidenotes `max-width: 40%`, `line-height: 1.42`, face `et-book`.

**Butterick, Summary of key rules** (verbatim):
- "Point size should be 10–12 points in printed documents, **15–25 pixels on the web**"
- "Line spacing should be **120–145%** of the point size"
- "The average line length should be **45–90 characters** (including spaces)"
- "Use bold or italic as little as possible, and not together"
- "Never underline, except perhaps for web links"
- "All caps are fine for less than one line of text"
- "Use **5–12% extra letterspacing** with all caps and small caps"
- "If you don't have real small caps, don't use them at all"
- "In documents exceeding three pages, limit exclamation points to one"
- Curly quotes; one space between sentences; proper ellipsis; apostrophes point downward; kerning always on

### Tracking that inverts by size (Asterisk)

```
display / large:  -0.05em, -0.03em, -0.02em, -0.01em
small / caps:     +0.01em, +0.02em   (with text-transform: uppercase)
```

This inversion — tighter as type grows, looser as type shrinks — is the single most reliable typographer's fingerprint. Generated CSS either omits tracking or applies one value globally.

### Typeface systems, verified from font files and `font-family` declarations

| Property | Faces actually loaded |
|---|---|
| Works in Progress | **Editor** (Regular/Bold/Italic) + **GT America Mono** (Light/Bold) |
| Asterisk | **Atlas Grotesk** (sans) + **Noe Text** (serif) + **Noe Standard** (display serif) |
| Stripe Press | **Ivar Display / Ivar Headline / Ivar Text** (one superfamily, three optical sizes) |
| Aeon | **Academica** (book roman+italic, bold+italic) + **Atlas Grotesk** (light/regular/bold + italics) + **Atlas Typewriter** + **Stratos** (medium/semilight) + **PP Right Grotesk Wide Medium** |
| The Pudding | **Atlas Grotesk** + **Atlas Typewriter** + **Tiempos Text** + **Gooper SemiCondensed** |
| Nautilus | **Freight Sans** (Book/SemiBold) + **Freight Display** (Book) |
| transformer-circuits.pub | **Styrene A** (Regular/Medium) + **Tiempos Text** (Regular/Italic/Medium) |
| Epoch AI | **Messina Sans** (Regular/SemiBold) |
| New Yorker | **TNYAdobeCaslonPro** + **Irvin Text / Irvin Heading** (bespoke) + **Neutraface New Yorker** + **Graphik** + **Lora** + **Lato** |
| Distill | HoeflerText / Georgia serif stack |
| Our World in Data | Lato Latin |
| gwern.net | **Source Serif 4** + **Source Sans 3** + **IBM Plex Mono** + 6 historical initial faces |

**Not one of them uses a single typeface. Not one of them uses Inter as its reading face.** (rsms.me does use Inter — because Rasmus Andersson designed it. That's authorship, not default.)

### gwern's craft layer

```css
font-feature-settings: 'ss01';
font-feature-settings: 'ss02', 'ss03';
font-variant-caps: small-caps;
font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;
font-variant-numeric: lining-nums;
hyphens: none;
```
plus rotating drop caps from `Cheshire Initials`, `Deutsche Zierschrift`, `Goudy Initialen`, `Great Primer Uncials`, `Kanzlei Initialen`, `Yinit`.

His sidenote essay quotes Bringhurst: *"Sidenotes give more life and variety to the page and are the easiest of all to find and read."* It also documents the mandatory caveat: sidenotes collide below ~1024px, so a fallback (Tufte-CSS pop-in, inline expansion, or endnote collapse) has to be decided up front.

---

## A) BANNED — dead-giveaway signals

### A1. Colour
1. Any purple→blue / indigo→violet gradient. Specifically ban the hexes `#6366F1`, `#4F46E5`, `#818CF8`, `#8B5CF6`, `#A855F7` and Tailwind's `indigo-*` / `violet-*` scales. **Delete the `colors` key from the Tailwind theme entirely** rather than extending it, so there is no fallback.
2. Purple→cyan, blue→teal, or any two-stop gradient as a page or hero background.
3. Gradient text (`bg-clip-text` on a gradient) anywhere.
4. Animated gradient blobs, mesh gradients, radial "aurora" glows behind the hero.
5. Coloured glows and coloured `box-shadow` (`shadow-indigo-500/50` and relatives).
6. **Cream/beige ground + rust/terracotta accent used together** — the 2026 signature. Cream alone is fine; cream *plus* rust *plus* italic serif is not.
7. "Tasteful, slightly askew" desaturated mid-century primaries as a set.
8. Pure `#000000` body text on pure `#FFFFFF` at full-page scale.
9. Permanent dark mode with medium-grey (`#9CA3AF`-ish) body text.
10. More than one chromatic accent unless each one encodes something (as WiP's do, per topic).

### A2. Type
11. Inter as the only typeface. (Also: Inter for headings *and* body *and* UI.)
12. The named AI stacks: **Space Grotesk + Instrument Serif**, **Geist**, **Playfair Display over a clean sans**, **Manrope + Outfit**.
13. A single serif-italic accent word inside an otherwise-sans headline ("Research that **matters**").
14. Tracked-out all-caps eyebrow labels above every section (`SELECTED WORK` / `OUR RESEARCH` at `+0.15em`). Small caps are the grown-up version.
15. One global `letter-spacing` value applied at all sizes; or no tracking anywhere.
16. Uniform `line-height: 1.5` on everything from 13px captions to 56px headlines.
17. Fake small caps (`font-variant: small-caps` on a face without real SC), fake italics (`font-style: italic` synthesised), fake bold.
18. Straight quotes `"` `'`, hyphens used as dashes, `...` instead of `…`.
19. Measure over ~90 characters, or under ~45.
20. More than three weights of one family doing hierarchy work that size and space should do.

### A3. Layout & components
21. Centred hero: big headline, one-line subhead, two CTA buttons side by side.
22. A pill "badge" directly above the H1 ("🚀 Now accepting PhD students").
23. Three-across feature grid: icon + title + two lines of text, `repeat(3, 1fr)`, equal card heights.
24. `rounded-2xl` + `shadow-lg` + `p-6` + `bg-white` cards as the universal container.
25. Coloured left-border stripes on cards.
26. Numbered `1 · 2 · 3` "how it works" step sequences.
27. Stat banners / animated counters (`50+ Publications`, `12 Students`, `8 Projects`).
28. Testimonial carousels, logo walls, "as featured in" strips.
29. Glassmorphism / frosted translucent panels over imagery — contrast becomes dynamic and can't be verified against WCAG AA.
30. Every gap on an 8pt grid with zero optical corrections and zero asymmetry.
31. Perfectly symmetric everything: every section centred, every container `max-w-7xl mx-auto`.
32. Full-bleed dark hero → white section → dark section → white section alternation.
33. Sticky translucent-blur nav bar with a `backdrop-filter`.

### A4. Icons & imagery
34. A grid of interchangeable thin-line Lucide/Heroicons/Feather icons standing in for ideas (droplet = hydrology, cloud = climate, chart = data).
35. **Emoji as section markers, nav icons or bullet glyphs.** Also an accessibility problem — judges in the 2025 academic-website contest flagged exactly this on an otherwise-winning site.
36. Stock photography: "diverse group of people looking at a laptop in an impossibly well-lit office."
37. Abstract 3D blobs, floating glass shapes, isometric illustrations.
38. **Any AI-generated image.** For a hydrologist this is a credibility problem, not merely a taste one. 2026 tells that still work: garbled background text (signage, book spines, packaging), cloned faces in crowds, inconsistent shadow directions, absent C2PA/SynthID provenance.
39. Duotone-overlaid photographs in the accent colour.

### A5. Motion
40. Scroll-triggered fade/slide-in on body content. NN/g participant, verbatim: *"I don't like how everything comes together when I'm scrolling down. … I hate that it has to load every single section. Sometimes I just want to see information there without having to see a cool little movement."*
41. Staggered `AOS`-style reveals with per-child delays.
42. Count-up number animations.
43. Bounce/scale-up on every hover.
44. Marquee / ticker text bars — explicitly named in the 2026 AI-tell list.
45. Parallax on anything.
46. Any motion that replays on back-navigation. (NN/g: fire once, ever.)

### A6. Copy & voice
47. "Elevate / Unlock / Empower / Transform / Harness / Leverage / Streamline your X."
48. "Build the future of…", "Your all-in-one platform", "Scale without limits", "Build faster. Ship smarter."
49. "It's not just X — it's Y."
50. "In today's fast-paced world", "in the ever-evolving landscape of", "at the intersection of".
51. Ström-Awn's expansion artifacts: *delve, intricate, tapestry, multifaceted*; and the post-ChatGPT frequency spikes *commendable, meticulous, pivotal, showcasing, robust, seamless, comprehensive, holistic, nuanced, cutting-edge, transformative, groundbreaking*.
52. The setup → payoff → signposted-takeaway paragraph shape ("This matters because…").
53. Two-noun abstract feature names ("Seamless Integration", "Data-Driven Insights", "Holistic Approach").
54. Third-person hagiography: "Dr. Regonda is a leading researcher advancing our understanding of…"
55. "Let's connect!", "Feel free to reach out!", "Excited to share…", exclamation points generally.
56. Any sentence with no proper noun, no number and no date in it.
57. Perfectly parallel tricolons everywhere ("faster, simpler, smarter").

---

## B) SIGNALS OF A REAL DESIGNER

### B1. Type
1. **Two families with a stated argument**, plus a mono for metadata. Each has a job you can name in one sentence.
2. A family chosen for a *reason you can say out loud* — foundry, provenance, language support, a specific letterform. "Editor, from the Indian Type Foundry" is a reason. "A modern sans" is not.
3. **Optical sizing**: `font-optical-sizing: auto`, or a display cut vs. a text cut (Stripe Press's Ivar Display / Headline / Text).
4. **Tracking that inverts with size**: negative on display, positive on small caps/labels (Asterisk: −0.05em → +0.02em).
5. Real small caps, real italics, real tabular figures. `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on the publications and student tables so years form a column.
6. `font-feature-settings` used at all (`ss01`, `liga`, `onum`/`lnum`).
7. Measure declared in `ch` and held to 45–90 characters; body 18–20px; leading ~1.5–1.6 on body, ~1.15–1.25 on display.
8. Line-height as a bare number, and never the same value for a 13px caption and a 48px headline.
9. `text-wrap: balance` on headings, `text-wrap: pretty` on paragraphs.
10. Curly quotes, en/em dashes used correctly, `…` as a real character, non-breaking spaces before units and after §.
11. Hierarchy built from **size + space + one weight change**, not from four weights and three colours.

### B2. Colour & surface
12. **Near-monochrome plus one accent.** A grey ramp with semantic aliases (`--color-fg`, `--color-bg`, `--color-border`, `--color-accent`, `--color-focus`), exactly as The Pudding does.
13. A warm or cool near-black rather than `#000` (Stripe Press `#201819`; WiP `#121212`).
14. **Hairline rules at full strength** — `1px solid var(--c-text)`, not `rgba(0,0,0,.08)`. This is Asterisk's defining move.
15. `box-shadow` count in the whole stylesheet: 0–2.
16. `border-radius: 0` as the default; radius only where a photo or control genuinely needs it.
17. If accents are plural, each one **encodes** something (WiP's per-topic colours).

### B3. Layout
18. **One deliberate asymmetry, repeated**: `94fr 63fr`, `2fr 4fr 2fr 3fr 1.5fr`, `55% / 40%`. Never `repeat(3, 1fr)` for content.
19. A **functional margin column** — sidenotes, years, co-authors, dataset links, figure captions.
20. **Optical, not mathematical, spacing**: a heading sits closer to the paragraph it owns than to the block above; a caption hangs tighter than the grid says; a rule sits where it looks right, not where 8px says.
21. Optical alignment: hanging punctuation, negative text-indent on pull quotes, glyphs nudged 1px so they *look* aligned.
22. Print furniture borrowed honestly: running heads, folios, issue numbers, a colophon, rules that separate rather than boxes that contain.
23. Density with hierarchy. Real editorial pages are *information-rich*; generated minimalism is empty with huge padding.
24. Deliberate imperfection: a photograph slightly cropped off-grid, a rule that overshoots the column, a caption that hangs into the margin.

### B4. Content & voice
25. **Dates and specifics instead of adjectives**: "March 2024 · *Journal of Hydrology* · with A. Kumar · doi:10.1016/…" beats any sentence containing "cutting-edge".
26. Text that sounds like **one specific person**. Keep his own construction — *"after masters at the IIT Kanpur, I pursued PhD at the University of Colorado at Boulder"* — including the article quirk. Copy-edit for clarity, never for polish.
27. First person for the professor's own pages; third person only where convention demands (a formal bio for conference organisers).
28. Real photographs of real people and real places: the RAFT team in the field, gauges, drones, the Musi in flood, a whiteboard. Captioned with place and date.
29. Something that could only be on *this* site — real data. A hairline hydrograph from an actual record, drawn once and reused as the site's signature mark.
30. **One idiosyncratic ornament, applied systematically** (gwern's rotating drop caps are the model).
31. Honest negative space: sections that are short because there's little to say, rather than padded to match a sibling.

### B5. Craft & restraint
32. Self-hosted, subset `woff2` with `font-display: swap` and preloads for the two above-the-fold faces.
33. Visible, considered focus states (The Pudding maps `--color-focus` to its accent).
34. `prefers-reduced-motion` honoured, and almost nothing to reduce.
35. Motion budget near zero: a link underline transition, a focus ring, at most one first-load reveal.
36. Real 404, real print stylesheet, real `<title>` per page, real OG image that is a typographic card rather than a screenshot.
37. Semantic HTML that would still read correctly with CSS off — which for an academic site is most of the value.

---

## Print-inspired conventions worth borrowing specifically

- **Mono for metadata** (Works in Progress; The Pudding; Aeon's Atlas Typewriter). One decision, huge return.
- **Issue/serial numbering** on blog posts — turns an irregular blog into a series.
- **Running heads and folios**: a persistent, quiet line at the top or in the margin telling the reader where they are.
- **Sidenotes** (Tufte CSS body 55% / notes 40%) with a decided mobile fallback.
- **Drop caps** via `initial-letter: 3` (`-webkit-` prefixed; Chrome 110+, Safari 9+, no Firefox) as progressive enhancement.
- **Rules, not boxes.** Asterisk separates every list item with `border-bottom: 1px solid var(--c-text)` and never draws a card.
- **A colophon.** A short page naming the typefaces, the data sources for any charts, the photographers, and the build. This is the loudest possible "a person made this" signal, it costs 150 words, and every publication in the exemplar list has one.
- **Commissioned artwork per issue** (WiP commissions a different illustrator per issue). Cheaper local version: a different real field photograph as the header of each blog post.

---

## Project-specific: type and colour proposals with reasons

**Typeface option A (recommended — free, and has a reason):**
- Reading: **Erode** or **Sentient** — Indian Type Foundry, via Fontshare, ITF Free Font License (commercial + webfont use permitted; *verify the exact clause at https://www.fontshare.com/licenses/itf-ffl before shipping — I could not extract the clause text*).
- Interface: **Switzer** (ITF neo-grotesk).
- Metadata: a mono.
- **The reason, in the colophon:** ITF is an Indian foundry (Ahmedabad, 2009; 200+ families, 20 writing systems; Kohinoor in the Design Museum's permanent collection), and this is an Indian institution's site. Works in Progress — the closest reference in register — sets its entire magazine in ITF's *Editor*.

**Typeface option B (free, zero licence risk, proven at scale):** Source Serif 4 + Source Sans 3 + IBM Plex Mono — gwern's exact stack. Full italics, real small caps, tabular figures, variable.

**Typeface option C (paid, ~€200–600):** one licensed text face — Tiempos Text, Freight Text or Ivar Text — carrying the whole site.

**Colour:** near-black `#1A1918`–`#201819`; a paper ground that is **not** cream (a cool off-white around `#F4F5F3`, or a true white with the warm near-black doing the work); one rule grey; one metadata grey; **one** accent with a stated provenance. Water suggests blue — that's fine, but it must be a *named, sourced* blue (an IMD rainfall-classification value, a gauge-chart standard, a colour sampled from a specific photograph), not `#2563EB`. Write the provenance into the colophon.

---

## THE TASTE RUBRIC — 22 yes/no checks to run before shipping

Every answer must be **yes**. Any **no** is a blocker.

**Automated (grep the built CSS):**
1. Does `box-shadow` appear **≤2 times** in the entire stylesheet? *(Asterisk: 0. WiP: 2 in 214KB.)*
2. Is `border-radius` either `0` or absent everywhere except photos and form controls?
3. Are there **zero** occurrences of `linear-gradient`/`radial-gradient` on any text or full-width background?
4. Does the compiled CSS contain **zero** indigo/violet hexes (`#6366F1`, `#4F46E5`, `#818CF8`, `#8B5CF6`, `#A855F7`) and no Tailwind `indigo-*`/`violet-*` classes?
5. Are there **exactly two** text families plus one mono, and is the string `Inter` absent unless it is a deliberate, documented choice?
6. Does the section-level CSS contain **zero** instances of `repeat(3, 1fr)`, and at least one **uneven** `fr` ratio?
7. Is there **at least one** `font-variant-numeric`, `font-feature-settings` or `font-variant-caps` declaration?
8. Are `text-wrap: balance` (headings) and `text-wrap: pretty` (body) both present?
9. Do **at least three different** `letter-spacing` values exist, with negative values on display sizes and positive values on small/uppercase?
10. Is `prefers-reduced-motion` handled, and is the total count of scroll-triggered animations on body content **zero**?
11. Do **zero** emoji characters appear in any heading, nav item or button label?

**Visual / editorial (eyes on the page):**
12. Is the body text between **15 and 25px**, the measure between **45 and 90 characters**, and the leading between **120% and 145%**? *(Butterick)*
13. Is the palette **near-monochrome plus exactly one accent** — and can you state where that accent came from in one sentence?
14. Are separations drawn as **hairline rules in a real text colour**, never as `rgba(0,0,0,0.06)` shadows?
15. Does the page have **one deliberate asymmetry** that repeats across templates, and is the narrow column doing real work (years, co-authors, captions, notes)?
16. Take a screenshot, blur it to 20px. Is the composition still identifiable as **this** site and not any other academic site? *(If the blur shows a centred blob over three equal rectangles, fail.)*
17. Is every image a **real photograph of a real place or person**, with a caption naming place and date — with **zero** stock and **zero** AI-generated imagery anywhere on the site?
18. Is there **one idiosyncratic detail** — a device, a numbering system, a margin mark, a chart drawn from real data — that appears on every page and could not exist on any other site?

**Copy (read it aloud):**
19. Does **every** sentence on the homepage contain at least one proper noun, number or date?
20. Read the bio aloud in the professor's voice. Does it sound like **him** — first person, his institutions, his phrasing, his slight article quirks — rather than like a press release?
21. Search the full text for: *elevate, unlock, empower, leverage, harness, streamline, seamless, robust, cutting-edge, transformative, holistic, ever-evolving, delve, tapestry, multifaceted, at the intersection of, passionate about, let's connect.* **Zero hits?** And is there **at most one** exclamation point in the whole site?
22. Is there a **colophon** naming the typefaces (and why), the data sources for any chart, the photographers, and the build — and does reading it make it obvious a person made deliberate choices?

## Deterministic check script (drop into the repo)

The developersdigest piece recommends "Playwright-based deterministic CSS checks against your pages (no LLM judges)." A simpler version that catches most of it:

```bash
CSS=dist/assets/*.css
echo "box-shadow: $(grep -oc 'box-shadow' $CSS)"      # want <= 2
echo "gradients:  $(grep -oc 'linear-gradient\|radial-gradient' $CSS)"  # want 0
echo "3-col:      $(grep -oc 'repeat(3, *1fr)' $CSS)"  # want 0
echo "indigo:     $(grep -oiEc '#(6366f1|4f46e5|818cf8|8b5cf6|a855f7)|indigo|violet' $CSS)"  # want 0
echo "families:   $(grep -oiE 'font-family:[^;}]*' $CSS | sort -u | wc -l)"  # want ~3
echo "tracking:   $(grep -oiE 'letter-spacing: *-?[0-9.]+em' $CSS | sort -u | wc -l)"  # want >= 3
echo "radius!=0:  $(grep -oiE 'border-radius: *[1-9]' $CSS | wc -l)"  # want small
grep -rioE 'elevate|unlock|empower|leverage|harness|streamline|seamless|cutting-edge|ever-evolving|delve|tapestry|multifaceted' src/content/  # want empty
```

Commit a `DESIGN.md` alongside it holding the palette tokens, the two typefaces and their reasons, the layout ratio, and the banned list — so that when content is edited over the next five years (or when another model touches the code), the defaults can't creep back in.
